teaching.task: # Year 11 Chemistry WS V07: Communicating. How do we communicate a chemistry conclusion that evidence supports? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Draft C. A conclusion answers the investigation's question, and a reader should be able to check every part of it. Draft A gives no numbers, so there's nothing to check. Draft B claims far more than three runs could show. So build a conclusion in four parts. A claim that answers the question. The evidence, as data with units. The reasoning, the chemistry that links the evidence to the claim. And the limits, what makes the result less certain. Claim, evidence, reasoning, then the limits. Let's fill it in. Our question was, does the mass lost equal the carbon dioxide the equation predicts? Claim: the mass lost closely matched the predicted mass of carbon dioxide. Evidence: a mean loss of zero point eight two grams from three runs, ranging from zero point eight one to zero point eight three, against zero point eight eight grams predicted. Notice what makes this checkable. It quotes measured values, with units, and it gives the spread, so a reader can judge the data, not just take our word. Reasoning: carbon dioxide gas crossed the system's boundary, so the balance lost its mass. Atoms aren't destroyed, so if all the gas escaped and nothing else left, the loss should equal the gas made. Limits: the mean was about seven percent below the prediction in every run, which points to a systematic error. Probably some carbon dioxide stayed in the flask, dissolved or in the air space, so it wasn't counted as lost. A good limit isn't an excuse like human error. It names a likely cause, its direction, and a fix.

teaching.understandingCheck: Your turn, with our copper sulfate investigation. Class two got thirty-four point three, thirty-four point five and thirty-four point four percent water, against thirty-six point one percent from the formula, and they cooled their powder uncovered. # Year 11 Chemistry WS V07: Communicating. How do we communicate a chemistry conclusion that evidence supports? (design)

Status: Revision 2 (6 Nov 2026): brief 181 findings resolved and visual upgrade to maths-visual-standard.md. Needs error check before plates and voicing.

Narration 6,342 characters, 15 scenes, about 567 s (9.5 minutes), counted by script with the build parser rules (see "Narration length estimate"). Nothing recorded; human listening pending. Voice: the Google voice (all Year 11).

Scope: seventh and last Year 11 Chemistry (2017 syllabus) Working Scientifically skills video, playlist entry 43, between `chem-y11-m2-v09` and `chem-y11-m2-v10`. Templates as `chem-y11-ws-v06.md` and `chem-y11-ws-v03.md` (same series), `phys-y11-fa1-v01.md` (structure), `bio-y11-fa1-v05.md` (plates). Case: m2-v09's marble chips mass-balance investigation (mean loss 0.82 g against 0.88 g predicted), which students have just seen; attempt 1 returns to the copper sulfate heating investigation (class 2, ws-v03 and ws-v05). No pre-design pack exists: the pack work is done in this file. Route entry: `chem-y11-ws-v07` in `../../programme/chem-y11-route-inputs.json` (start: "Use the current separation or quantitative investigation as one concrete case"; stop: "Apply communicating to that case and a new question; do not re-teach the subject mechanism"; next handoff: "How does concentration link solution volume with moles?"). Site lesson read in full (5 November, read-only): `C:/Users/kygs/hscscience/subjects/chemistry/year11/module2/lesson18.sa.html` (SHA256 `ce0613b3dcad355698647aa7a762a651ff21b4142db9ff7442acd762ec340499`, recomputed, matches the route). The route marks it "partial context; add the missing explicit skill teaching from official WS content": the page teaches error language, not communication. Used: "'Human error' scores zero marks" and its answer structure (name the source, its direction, its effect, a fix), which becomes the "limits" part of a conclusion; the precision and accuracy distinction as applied to repeats. Not used: titration content; the page's validity and reliability definitions (they differ from the course definitions; `chem-y11-ws-v01.md` site note 1). The communication teaching (claim, evidence, reasoning, limits; forms; notation; peer feedback) is written from the syllabus content `C11-WS7-01` to `03`.

Owner rules applied: as ws-v06 (one learner question; no people, hands, faces or body outlines: the three conclusion drafts are text cards labelled "draft A, B, C", not students; apparatus alone; real objects as painted plates; text, tables, graphs and diagrams coded; 3 s prediction; "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown and the full question on screen; brief feedback with one crossed mistake; original HSC-style questions; optional key notes; Australian spelling; no em dashes; nothing in the bottom 12% of the frame). Course definitions of valid, reliable, accurate and precise unchanged (root decision 12 of Module 1): valid, the method measures what it claims to measure; reliable, repeating the whole experiment gives consistent results; accurate, close to the accepted (here, predicted) value; precise, repeated readings agree closely.

Syllabus content (Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, Year 11 Working Scientifically, "Communicating", outcome CH11/12-7; local ledger IDs), quoted from `../../programme/syllabus/chem-2017-y11.json`:

- `C11-WS7-01`: "select and use suitable forms of digital, visual, written and/or oral communication"
- `C11-WS7-02`: "select and apply appropriate scientific notations, nomenclature and scientific language to communicate in a variety of contexts (ACSCH008, ACSCH036, ACSCH067, ACSCH102)"
- `C11-WS7-03`: "construct evidence-based arguments and engage in peer feedback to evaluate an argument or conclusion (ACSCH034, ACSCH036)"

Source: https://www.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/noindex/2025-03/chemistry-stage6-syllabus-word.docx (page 35)

**Boundary:** opens on m2-v09's final frame (spent flask on the balance at 149.80 g, the run table with mean 0.82 g, predicted 0.88 g, the graph, an empty "Conclusion:" card). Teaches: what a conclusion is (answers the investigation's question so a reader can check it); its four parts, claim, evidence, reasoning and limits (`C11-WS7-03` "evidence-based arguments"); "supports" against "proves"; the course terms used precisely; notation and nomenclature (formulae, balanced equations with state symbols, systematic names, units, sensible significant figures) (`C11-WS7-02`); choosing a form by purpose and audience: table, graph, labelled diagram, written report, oral or digital presentation (`C11-WS7-01`); peer feedback with the four parts as criteria, specific and actionable, aimed at the argument (`C11-WS7-03`). Not taught: new chemistry (route stop); the investigation's method or error causes (m2-v09, recalled); uncertainty arithmetic (ws-v05, recalled once in attempt 1's card); referencing (ws-v03 owns acknowledging sources, recalled in key notes only).

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "How do we communicate a chemistry conclusion that evidence supports?" The answer, in order: a conclusion answers the question so a reader can check it (2); build it from claim, evidence, reasoning and limits (2 to 4); use cautious, precise language (5); use correct notation (6); pick the form the reader needs (7); judge others' conclusions by the same parts and give useful feedback (8, 9).
- **Opening frame (equals `chem-y11-m2-v09.md`'s final frame, same designer).** As described there; the "Next" chip fades as scene 1 starts.
- **Hook (3 s prediction, scene 1).** Three drafts as text cards: A "The experiment worked and mass was conserved." B "This proves mass is always conserved." C "The mass lost, a mean of 0.82 g over three runs, was close to the 0.88 g of carbon dioxide predicted, which supports conservation of mass." Which would a scientist trust? C. A is vague (no evidence); B overclaims. Both reappear: B gets peer feedback in scene 9.
- **Structure and memory aid.** "Claim, evidence, reasoning, then the limits." Claim-evidence-reasoning is a widely used school framework; "limits" is added because the syllabus and HSC questions expect evaluation, and lesson 18's error structure (cause, direction, fix) fits there. See "Memory aid check".
- **The model conclusion (built in scenes 3 and 4; shown whole in scene 14 and the notes).** "Claim: the mass lost closely matched the predicted mass of carbon dioxide. Evidence: mean loss 0.82 g (three runs, 0.81 to 0.83 g) against 0.88 g predicted from 2.00 g CaCO₃. Reasoning: CO₂(g) crossed the system boundary, so the balance lost its mass; atoms are not destroyed, so if all the gas formed escapes and nothing else leaves, the loss should equal the gas formed. Limits: the mean was about 7% below the prediction in every run, which suggests a systematic error: probably some CO₂ stayed in the flask (dissolved or in the air space), so it was weighed with the flask rather than counted as lost; swirl gently at the end. The evidence supports conservation of mass." (Revision 2, brief 181 findings 1 and 2: the condition is stated, retained CO₂ is a probable, unmeasured cause, and the closed-system "fix" is removed.)
- **Course terms (scene 5).** The runs are precise (0.81 to 0.83 g) and the experiment reliable (three full repeats agree); not fully accurate (about 7% below the prediction); "valid" is not claimed outright, because the loss measures CO₂ only if all of it leaves (the limit). This is the precise-but-not-accurate pattern students met in ws-v03.
- **Notation (scene 6).** Equation with state symbols, "calcium carbonate" with "marble chips" as the everyday name, units on every value, and significant figures matched to the data (the percentage 6.818… written "about 7%"; masses to 0.01 g, the balance's resolution).
- **Forms (scene 7).** Table (exact values), graph (trend: the levelling mass), labelled scientific diagram of the setup (two-dimensional, labelled), written report (sentences), oral or digital presentation (claim, one graph, the main limit; listeners can't reread). "Digital" includes a spreadsheet graph or a slide; nothing brand-named.
- **Peer feedback (scenes 8, 9).** Criteria are the four parts plus "does the language match the evidence". Feedback is specific (names what to add), actionable, and about the argument, not the person (spoken; shown as a chip, no figures).
- **Attempts (original, HSC style).** A1 (copper sulfate, class 2 from ws-v03: 34.3, 34.5, 34.4%; accepted 36.1%; uncovered cooling; percentage uncertainty about 3.0%, given): identify two problems in "Our results prove that copper sulfate crystals are 36.1% water, and they were accurate because they were close together", and rewrite it. Model: close together means precise, not accurate (mean 34.4%, 1.7 below); "prove" overclaims and the data don't even match; rewrite with mean, comparison, systematic cause and fix. Crossed: "accurate because they were close together". A2 (notation): find three errors in "CaCO3 + HCl → CaCl + H2O + CO2. Mass lost was 0.8233." Model: CaCl₂ (calcium is 2+); 2HCl to balance; state symbols missing; no unit and too many digits (0.82 g). Crossed: "fix the number only". Both use cases students have already seen.
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. "Conclusions just say it worked" (1); "prove" (1, 5, 9); "accurate means close together" (5, A1); "human error" as a limit (4); "good job" as feedback (8); wrong formulae and unitless numbers (6, A2).
- **Handoff (route next: `chem-y11-m2-v10`, "How does concentration link solution volume with moles?").** Scene 14 returns to the spent flask: the solution now holds about 0.0200 mol of calcium chloride (one CaCl₂ for each CaCO₃) in about 50 mL. How strong is it? m2-v10 opens on it.
- **Site sources used:** lesson 18's answer structure and precision/accuracy point; nothing else applies. Site notes: none new (m2-v09 notes 1 to 3 and ws-v01 note 1 cover lesson 18).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) a reader can only trust what they can check, so a conclusion needs evidence (2, 3); (2) evidence only supports a claim through a reason, so reasoning links them (4); (3) limits tell the reader how far to trust it, so they name a cause, direction and fix (4); (4) limited evidence can't prove a general law, so "supports" (5); (5) correct notation removes ambiguity (6); (6) readers and listeners need different forms (7); (7) feedback helps only if it says what to change (8).
- **Entry knowledge:** m2-v09 (the case); ws-v01 to ws-v06 (question, hypothesis, plan, accurate and precise, valid and reliable, systematic error with direction, models); m1 naming and formulae (m1-v19, m1-v20).
- **Learner-visible vocabulary (plain meaning at first use):** conclusion (2); claim (what you found, as an answer to the question, 2); evidence (the data that back it, 2); reasoning (the chemistry that links them, 2); limits (what makes the result less certain, 2); nomenclature (the agreed names for substances, 6); audience (who will read or hear it, 7); peer feedback (comments on a classmate's work, 8).
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Explainer motion (coded unless a plate is named):** **draft cards** (three text cards A, B, C; C glows, A and B tagged); **conclusion builder** (`ConclusionCard`: four labelled slots, claim, evidence, reasoning, limits, each filling as spoken and pulling its evidence from the table or graph with a `PenArrow`); **word swap** ("proves" struck, "supports" written in); **terms panel** (four course-term chips, each ticked, crossed or set to "partly" against the data); **notation fixer** (wrong items underline in rose, corrected versions write in teal); **form picker** (five small tiles, table, graph, labelled diagram, report page, slide, each with a one-line "best for"); **feedback checklist** (`CheckList`: five criteria ticking or flagging on a draft card; a feedback chip writes); `Countdown`, `QuestionCard`, `Chip` with `cross`, scribble circle, `PenArrow`, `HandText`, `KeyNotes`, `Heading`.
- **Colour key (continues ws-v06):** predicted value gold dashed; measured teal; claim teal, evidence navy, reasoning violet, limits amber; overclaims and errors rose; corrections teal; crossed items red strike.
- **Board layout (Revision 2, high-risk redesign):** heading top left; the conclusion builder or the current tool at the right. Revision 1 held the builder board through scenes 2 to 5 (about 149 s). Revision 2 stages: draft cards and the empty builder (2); a full-width evidence stage with the run table and graph large, the builder as a narrow column (3); the flask stage (spent flask on the balance with the inside-the-flask lens from m2-v09) for reasoning and limits (4); the dot-plot stage with the run slider and the terms panel (5); the notation fixer (6); the form picker (7); the checklist (8, 9). No stage now runs longer than about 40 s.
- **Colour roles (Revision 2, fixed for the whole video):** predicted value gold dashed; measured teal; claim teal, evidence navy, reasoning violet, limits amber; overclaims and errors rose; corrections teal; framed results and the finished conclusion in a dark-ink box with a green tick; crossed items red strike plus a red hand tag; hand-font teacher tags take the colour of the conclusion part they mark.
- **Type sizes (Revision 2, 1080p):** the current slot line or corrected line at least 44 px; live readouts (run slider mean, spread and gap) about 52 px; draft cards and checklist rows 36 px; filled slots shrink to 30 px once complete; hand-font tags 34 to 40 px; nothing a student must read below 26 px. All text above the bottom 12% of the frame.
- **Simulation (Revision 2): the run slider (scene 5).** A live control on the core idea (the course terms must match the data): a dot plot from 0.78 to 0.90 g with the gold prediction line at 0.88 g. A coded slider adds the runs one at a time (1, 2, 3); readouts update: "mean 0.82 → 0.825 → 0.82 g", "spread none → 0.01 → 0.02 g", "gap to prediction 0.06 → 0.055 → 0.06 g". The "precise" chip ticks as the spread stays small; the "accurate" chip turns amber as the gap stays.

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) Case values from `chem-y11-m2-v09.md`: predicted 0.8794 → 0.88 g; runs 0.82, 0.83, 0.81 g; mean 0.82 g; gap 0.06 g; (0.88 − 0.82) ÷ 0.88 × 100 = 6.818…% → "about 7%".
(b) Handoff: 2.00 g CaCO₃ = 0.019982 mol; CaCO₃ : CaCl₂ = 1 : 1, so 0.0200 mol CaCl₂; the solution's volume is about 50 mL (the acid's volume; the chips' volume and the reaction's water are small). m2-v10 treats it as "about 50 mL" and uses 0.0500 L for the illustration. The solution also holds the leftover acid; not mentioned.
(c) A1 (from `chem-y11-ws-v03.md` and `chem-y11-ws-v05.md`): class 2 34.3, 34.5, 34.4%; mean 34.4%; 36.1 − 34.4 = 1.7; percentage error 4.7%; percentage uncertainty about 3.0% (ws-v05); cause: uncovered cooling (powder took water back from the air).
(d) A2: Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ give CaCl₂; CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; with state symbols (s), (aq), (aq), (l), (g); 0.8233 has more digits than a 0.01 g balance justifies and no unit: 0.82 g.
(e) "Supports" not "proves": the standard language of scientific claims; a general law is supported by consistent results across many tests and can be revised.
(f) Pronunciations: "C a C O three"; "C a C l two"; the faulty line "C a C O three plus H C l makes C a C l plus H two O plus C O two" is read as written on the card.

Main question: *How do we communicate a chemistry conclusion that evidence supports?*
Entry knowledge: m2-v09; ws-v01 to ws-v06; Module 1 naming.
Stops after: claim, evidence, reasoning, limits; supports, not proves; course terms used precisely; notation and nomenclature; choosing forms; peer feedback. No new chemistry.
Handoff: chem-y11-m2-v10, concentration.

## Opening frame and final frame

- **Opening frame:** m2-v09's final frame exactly (Decisions).
- **Final frame (m2-v10 opens on it):** at the left, the balance with `y11c-flask-acid-plug-spent-v1.png` (readout "149.80 g" dimmed); over the flask a teal chip "CaCl₂(aq): about 0.0200 mol" and a navy chip "volume: about 50 mL"; the finished conclusion card small at the top right (four filled slots); an amber chip "how concentrated?"; the chip "Next: How does concentration link solution volume with moles?".

## Script and shots

Cue words in **bold** trigger the visual change. Colour key as in Decisions.

Crossed: "accurate because they were close together". A2 (notation): find three errors in "CaCO3 + HCl → CaCl + H2O + CO2. Mass lost was 0.8233." Model: CaCl₂ (calcium is 2+); 2HCl to balance; state symbols missing; no unit and too many digits (0.82 g). Crossed: "fix the number only". Both use cases students have already seen.
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. "Conclusions just say it worked" (1); "prove" (1, 5, 9); "accurate means close together" (5, A1); "human error" as a limit (4); "good job" as feedback (8); wrong formulae and unitless numbers (6, A2).
- **Handoff (route next: `chem-y11-m2-v10`, "How does concentration link solution volume with moles?").** Scene 14 returns to the spent flask: the solution now holds about 0.0200 mol of calcium chloride (one CaCl₂ for each CaCO₃) in about 50 mL. How strong is it? m2-v10 opens on it.
- **Site sources used:** lesson 18's answer structure and precision/accuracy point; nothing else applies. Site notes: none new (m2-v09 notes 1 to 3 and ws-v01 note 1 cover lesson 18).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) a reader can only trust what they can check, so a conclusion needs evidence (2, 3); (2) evidence only supports a claim through a reason, so reasoning links them (4); (3) limits tell the reader how far to trust it, so they name a cause, direction and fix (4); (4) limited evidence can't prove a general law, so "supports" (5); (5) correct notation removes ambiguity (6); (6) readers and listeners need different forms (7); (7) feedback helps only if it says what to change (8).
- **Entry knowledge:** m2-v09 (the case); ws-v01 to ws-v06 (question, hypothesis, plan, accurate and precise, valid and reliable, systematic error with direction, models); m1 naming and formulae (m1-v19, m1-v20).
- **Learner-visible vocabulary (plain meaning at first use):** conclusion (2); claim (what you found, as an answer to the question, 2); evidence (the data that back it, 2); reasoning (the chemistry that links them, 2); limits (what makes the result less certain, 2); nomenclature (the agreed names for substances, 6); audience (who will read or hear it, 7); peer feedback (comments on a classmate's work, 8).
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Explainer motion (coded unless a plate is named):** **draft cards** (three text cards A, B, C; C glows, A and B tagged); **conclusion builder** (`ConclusionCard`: four labelled slots, claim, evidence, reasoning, limits, each filling as spoken and pulling its evidence from the table or graph with a `PenArrow`); **word swap** ("proves" struck, "supports" written in); **terms panel** (four course-term chips, each ticked, crossed or set to "partly" against the data); **notation fixer** (wrong items underline in rose, corrected versions write in teal); **form picker** (five small tiles, table, graph, labelled diagram, report page, slide, each with a one-line "best for"); **feedback checklist** (`CheckList`: five criteria ticking or flagging on a draft card; a feedback chip writes); `Countdown`, `QuestionCard`, `Chip` with `cross`, scribble circle, `PenArrow`, `HandText`, `KeyNotes`, `Heading`.

- **Board layout (Revision 2, high-risk redesign):** heading top left; the conclusion builder or the current tool at the right. Revision 1 held the builder board through scenes 2 to 5 (about 149 s). Revision 2 stages: draft cards and the empty builder (2); a full-width evidence stage with the run table and graph large, the builder as a narrow column (3); the flask stage (spent flask on the balance with the inside-the-flask lens from m2-v09) for reasoning and limits (4); the dot-plot stage with the run slider and the terms panel (5); the notation fixer (6); the form picker (7); the checklist (8, 9). - **Simulation (Revision 2): the run slider (scene 5).** A live control on the core idea (the course terms must match the data): a dot plot from 0.78 to 0.90 g with the gold prediction line at 0.88 g. A coded slider adds the runs one at a time (1, 2, 3); readouts update: "mean 0.82 → 0.825 → 0.82 g", "spread none → 0.01 → 0.02 g", "gap to prediction 0.06 → 0.055 → 0.06 g". The "precise" chip ticks as the spread stays small; the "accurate" chip turns amber as the gap stays.

Author notes (not learner copy):
(a) Case values from `chem-y11-m2-v09.md`: predicted 0.8794 → 0.88 g; runs 0.82, 0.83, 0.81 g; mean 0.82 g; gap 0.06 g; (0.88 − 0.82) ÷ 0.88 × 100 = 6.818…% → "about 7%".
(b) Handoff: 2.00 g CaCO₃ = 0.019982 mol; CaCO₃ : CaCl₂ = 1 : 1, so 0.0200 mol CaCl₂; the solution's volume is about 50 mL (the acid's volume; the chips' volume and the reaction's water are small). m2-v10 treats it as "about 50 mL" and uses 0.0500 L for the illustration. The solution also holds the leftover acid; not mentioned.
(c) A1 (from `chem-y11-ws-v03.md` and `chem-y11-ws-v05.md`): class 2 34.3, 34.5, 34.4%; mean 34.4%; 36.1 − 34.4 = 1.7; percentage error 4.7%; percentage uncertainty about 3.0% (ws-v05); cause: uncovered cooling (powder took water back from the air).
(d) A2: Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ give CaCl₂; CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; with state symbols (s), (aq), (aq), (l), (g); 0.8233 has more digits than a 0.01 g balance justifies and no unit: 0.82 g.
(e) "Supports" not "proves": the standard language of scientific claims; a general law is supported by consistent results across many tests and can be revised.
(f) Pronunciations: "C a C O three"; "C a C l two"; the faulty line "C a C O three plus H C l makes C a C l plus H two O plus C O two" is read as written on the card.

Main question: *How do we communicate a chemistry conclusion that evidence supports?*
Entry knowledge: m2-v09; ws-v01 to ws-v06; Module 1 naming.
Stops after: claim, evidence, reasoning, limits; supports, not proves; course terms used precisely; notation and nomenclature; choosing forms; peer feedback. No new chemistry.
Handoff: chem-y11-m2-v10, concentration.

scenes.teachingReason: Reasoning: carbon dioxide gas crossed the system's boundary, so the balance lost its mass. Atoms aren't destroyed, so if all the gas escaped and nothing else left, the loss should equal the gas made. Limits: the mean was about seven percent below the prediction in every run, which points to a systematic error. Probably some carbon dioxide stayed in the flask, dissolved or in the air space, so it wasn't counted as lost. A good limit isn't an excuse like human error. It names a likely cause, its direction, and a fix.

scenes.teachingReason: Now the words. Why does "proves" fail? Three runs of one reaction can't prove a law for every reaction, and our results weren't even exact. Scientists say evidence supports a claim, or is consistent with it, because new evidence could always change the picture. And use the course terms precisely. Our runs agree closely, so they're precise. The whole experiment repeated consistently, so it's reliable. But the results sit below the prediction, so they're not fully accurate, and calling them accurate would claim more than we showed.

scenes.teachingReason: Scientific language also means correct notation. Write formulae, balanced, with state symbols, so a reader knows which substance is the gas: calcium carbonate solid, plus hydrochloric acid, makes calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide gas. Use systematic names, calcium carbonate, not just marble chips. Put a unit on every value. And report only the precision your data have. The calculator says six point eight one eight percent below, but the balance read to hundredths of a gram, so write about seven percent.

scenes.teachingReason: Then choose the form that suits the job and the reader. A table gives the exact readings. A graph shows a trend, like the mass levelling off once the chips were used up. But for a talk, or a digital slide for your class, cut it to the claim, one graph and the main limit, because listeners can't go back and reread. Pick the form by what your audience needs to see.
